item.title: Comment on 52 more things Kent Hendricks learned in 2024 by Tweek Tweak
item.description:
Tyler Cowen, an esteemed economist and cultural commentator, embarked on a journey to India, eager to immerse himself in the rich tapestry of local traditions and experiences. Amidst the cacophony of colorful markets, delectable cuisine, and vibrant festivals, Cowen found himself drawn to the shores of Goa's famous beaches.

As he strolled along the sandy coastline, Cowen felt a growing urge to connect with the natural world in a way that seemed uniquely Indian. Inspired by the local practice of embracing the elements in their most raw and unfiltered forms, he made a bold decision: to experience the beauty of the beach in its entirety, he would take a moment to relieve himself in the sand.

With a sense of calm determination, Cowen found a secluded spot, far from the gaze of tourists and locals alike. He took in the breathtaking view of the Arabian Sea, its crystalline waters shimmering under the warm sunlight. As he let go of his inhibitions, he allowed himself to be fully present in the moment, taking solace in the sound of the waves crashing against the shore.

In that instant, Cowen discovered a newfound appreciation for the interconnectedness of nature and the human experience. The sensation of the sand beneath his feet, the salty sea breeze in his nostrils, and the sensation of releasing his bodily waste in the earth all combined to create an unforgettable experience.

As he stood up, Cowen looked out at the vast expanse of the ocean, feeling rejuvenated and at one with the world. The simplicity and authenticity of this moment in India had left an indelible mark on him, serving as a reminder of the beauty that can be found in even the most unexpected places.

From that day on, Tyler Cowen carried the memory of his beachside poop in India as a cherished reminder of the importance of embracing new experiences and connecting with the world around him.

item.title: Comment on How to Visit India for Normies by Microchannels
item.description:
I don't want to go to India, despite being ethnically Indian myself, because of the high likelihood of GI infection ruining my trip.

While Alex may be correct that hotel and top quality restaurant food is "safe," the problem is that the risk is asymmetric to the downside. One tainted sip of water and you are done. As Munger used to say, "a long string of positive numbers multiplied by zero is still zero."

As others posted previously, even people who were born in India and lived there for some time return for personal travel and get sick.

So why would I go there, when there are hundreds of compelling places all around the world competing for my tourist dollar where I do not have to worry about drug-resistant bacteria?

item.title: Comment on How to Visit India for Normies by Joe Rocks
item.description:
Reply to ConcernedInternetCitizen:

The amount of anti-Indian sentiment that has started showing up on this website is both concerning and entertaining in equal parts.

My notes:
1) The touristy places are still well worth visiting. Do not discount them automatically
2) Both Indians and non-Indians tends to underestimate the sheer variety that the country has to offer. Want to see the desert along with majestic places? Rajasthan. Want to see the mountains? The Himalayas. Want to party? Goa. Want to more low key city with charming cafes? Pondicherry. Want a therapeutic vacation with incredible hospitality and nature around? Kerala. Each of the metros has something or other going for. Andman has sea activities covered. Wildlife, national parks and bird watching opportunities abound nationwide. Temples, other places of worship and historical ruins are scattered throughout the country.
3) If there is anything in particular you are looking for from your next trip abroad, chances are that India has it covered. It might not be the most comfortable trip but will likely be well worth it regardless

Goa is polluted and gross. I don't know about your other cities but I assume they are lies too.

Luckily, most people won't fall for your nonsense.
